Net neutrality is when your municipal government enforces a monopoly for a local Internet service provider, which inevitably leads to high prices and crappy service... So then, instead of driving your local politicians out of office and rescinding the grant, you septuple-down and try to get the federal government to start interfering with everyone's internet communications.

Yeah, that's my take on it. Here's a more generous description:

So the 'neutrality' part means that internet service providers (ISPs) should handle/treat all internet traffic equally--without prioritizing data flow from any particular source.

You can imagine that it takes far more bits (binary digits, ones and zeroes) to describe a feature length movie steamed from Netflix than it does to transcribe this text I'm writing. The engineers at your local ISP realize this and may take measures to improve your experience with Netflix so that you aren't waiting forever for movies to buffer. E.g., they might install some hardware to keep copies of the movies at their local data center so they don't have fetch them from across the country. They might write a rule in their routers that says if a data packet from Netflix is coming through at the same time as one from e.g., CNN.com for your neighbor; the one from Netflix gets to move through first and the CNN has to wait a bit. They might hire a trenching crew to install high bandwidth optical fiber directly between them and Netflix so there's less switching and back and forth through other intermediaries.

Net neutrality rules mean that the engineers are legally not allowed to improve the data flow from Netflix relative to CNN.com. I.e., any investment they make to improve their connection to Netflix must be matched by improvements to their connection to everyone on the internet.

This sounds somewhat reasonable if you trust the federal policy makers more than the engineers at your local ISP. You don't want anyone deciding that e.g., access to voat.co should be blocked because a majority of people find it offensive. The problem, in my view, is that I don't really trust either group but if there's competition, at l least I can choose the lesser of various evils. If we put all our eggs in the federal basket then we'll extend the same problems as the places with local monopolies to the rest of the country.

During the 90s and 2000s investment in all kinds of Internet infrastructure exploded prior to federal mandate.
